SCRAP METAL YARD PAYOUT CALCULATOR · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER · NOTHING UPLOADED

Which scrap yard nets you more? Payout after the drive, split or not, strip wire or not

For scrappers, electricians, plumbers, HVAC techs and demolition crews. Type the lots you are hauling and what two yards pay for each. The tool takes off fuel and vehicle cost, the minutes the trip takes at your hourly value, handling fees and grading deductions, then shows what the load nets at each yard, whether splitting it is worth a second trip, how much the other yard would have to pay to catch up, what a 10% or 20% price drop does, and whether stripping copper wire beats selling it insulated.

The method with a worked example: is a farther scrap yard worth the drive.

Wire: strip it or sell it insulated

How it is built

Units: everything is converted to pounds first: kilogram 2.2046 lb, short ton 2,000 lb, long ton 2,240 lb. Gross payout at a yard = pounds × that yard's price per pound × (1 − its grading deduction), summed over the lots. Trip cost = 2 × miles one way × cost per mile + round-trip minutes ÷ 60 × your hourly value + the yard's fee. Net = gross payout − trip cost.

Split: every lot goes to the yard that pays more for it, and both trips are charged; the tool shows the split only when each yard gets at least one lot. Catch-up: the percentage by which the lower-netting single yard would have to raise all its prices to equal the best single yard, with its trip cost unchanged. Price drop: every price cut by 10% or 20% with the trip costs held. Wire: stripped copper pounds × bare price − pounds × insulated price − strip hours × your hourly value; the break-even recovery is the copper share at which that is zero.

Common questions

Should I strip copper wire or sell it insulated?

Compare what the stripped copper sells for, minus the insulated price you give up, minus the value of your time. The calculator does it for your wire: pounds, insulated price, bare copper price, the share of the weight that comes out as copper, and minutes per pound. It also shows the recovery percentage where stripping stops paying, so you can test a different yard price or a faster stripper.

Is it worth driving farther to a yard that pays more per pound?

Only if the extra pay covers the extra miles, time and any handling fee. The calculator nets each yard after fuel and vehicle cost per mile, the minutes the round trip takes at your hourly value, and the fee, then tells you how much more the lower-netting yard would have to pay across the board to match the winner.

When does it pay to split a load between two yards?

Rarely for small loads. Each lot can pay more at one yard, but a split means two trips. The calculator sends every lot to its higher payer, charges both trips, and shows split only when it nets more than keeping everything at one yard.

How do I compare prices quoted per pound, per ton and per kilogram?

Pick the unit each price is quoted in and the unit you weighed in. The calculator converts everything to pounds (short ton 2,000 lb, long ton 2,240 lb, kilogram 2.2046 lb) before comparing, so a steel price per ton and a copper price per pound can sit in one load.

Does this show live scrap prices, and is it financial advice?

No. It has no price feed: you type the prices from each yard's board and they change daily. It is arithmetic on your numbers, not tax, legal or financial advice, and nothing you type is uploaded.

No warranty. This tool is provided free and as-is, without warranty of any kind, express or implied. It is arithmetic on the numbers you type, not tax, legal or financial advice, and it is not a price quote: scrap prices change daily and every yard sets its own grades and deductions. Use at your own risk. Check the weight ticket and payout with the yard before you sell.

Independent. Not affiliated with any scrap yard, recycler or price-reporting service, and none is named or ranked here.

Best-effort hosting, no SLA. These tools are free, experimental, and may be slow, broken, moved, or taken offline without notice. We do not promise uptime or backups of anything you enter.

Everything runs in your browser. Your numbers are never uploaded; there are no accounts, cookies, or analytics vendors. Anonymous feature events (load_run, example_loaded, text_copied, csv_downloaded, file_saved) are counted in this browser only, and you can switch that off below.

Is a farther scrap yard worth the drive?

The yard that pays more per pound is not always the yard that pays you more. The sample load below is 2205 lb of copper tube, aluminum, brass, stainless and steel. The far yard pays more for the copper and the brass; the near yard wins the whole load anyway. The prices are invented; use your own yards' boards.

The worked example

Five lots, 2205 lb in all. At the near yard (9 miles each way, 55 minutes for the round trip) the load grosses $754.95. At the far yard (22 miles, 85 minutes, a $5 handling fee) it grosses $741.70, which is less, because the far yard pays less for the aluminum, stainless and steel that make up most of the weight.

The drive: at $0.70 a mile the near trip costs $12.60 in truck and $22.92 in time at $25 an hour, $35.52 in all. The far trip costs $71.22. Netting each:

OptionNet
All at the near yard$719.43
All at the far yard$670.48
Split, each lot to its higher payer$666.97

That is $0.33 a pound netted at the near yard. The far yard would have to pay 6.6% more on everything to catch it.

Why splitting did not win

Sending the copper and brass to the far yard and the rest to the near one grosses $773.70, better than either yard alone. But it means driving both trips, and the second trip costs more than the extra the better prices bring in. A split pays when the lots with the biggest price gap are heavy or valuable enough to cover a second drive; here they are not.

If prices fall

Scrap prices move while a load sits in the truck. With every price down 10%, the best option nets $643.94; with every price down 20%, it nets $568.44. The trip costs do not fall with the prices, so a thin load can go from worth the drive to not worth it.

Strip the wire or sell it insulated?

Sixty pounds of insulated wire sells for $66.00 at $1.10 a pound. If 55% of the weight comes out as bare copper at $3.55, that copper sells for $117.15. Stripping takes 1.5 minutes a pound, 1.50 hours, which at $25 an hour is $37.50 of time. Stripping gains $13.65, or $34.10 extra for each hour at the stripper before any value on your time. It stops paying below 48.6% recovery; test your own wire by stripping a sample.

Run your own numbers: open the calculator.
